node-1.label: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a progressively enlarging purplish-red mass in the right lower limb since birth.

node-2.label: The mass measured approximately 5 × 5 cm with purplish-red discoloration and surrounding tissue swelling; physical examination revealed a 5 × 5 cm mass at the right knee joint that was warm to touch, of medium consistency, and well-defined; hemorrhagic spots were noted on the upper hard palate.

node-3.label: Past medical history, personal history, and immunization status were normal; there were no postnatal episodes of cyanosis, convulsions, or bleeding; family history was negative for congenital malformations, tumors, or hemorrhagic conditions.

node-4.label: Vital signs were stable, the infant was alert, and no abnormalities were detected in the central nervous, cardiovascular, or respiratory systems.

attrs.why: New laboratory evidence (platelet count 18 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.541 g/L, prolonged PT/APTT/TT, D-dimer 21.29, and anemia) and expert analyses indicate Kasabach-Merritt syndrome and favor kaposiform hemangioendothelioma/tufted angioma over a simple benign vascular tumor. The enhancing vascular mass on MRI still supports a vascular lesion, but the severe coagulopathy is atypical for a benign vascular tumor, so confidence is reduced from 0.55 to 0.15.

New severe thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, prolonged coagulation times, and elevated D-dimer are more consistent with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome than a vascular malformation. Although the congenital warm purplish mass remains compatible, the expert analyses and laboratory findings shift the diagnosis away from vascular malformation, reducing confidence from 0.20 to 0.05.

New laboratory findings of severe thrombocytopenia (18 × 10^9/L), low fibrinogen (0.541 g/L), prolonged PT/APTT/TT, elevated D-dimer (21.29), and anemia, together with the enhancing right inguinal/thigh vascular mass and palate hemorrhagic spots, strongly support Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. Both Pathologist and Radiologist expert analyses favor this diagnosis over simple benign vascular tumor, raising confidence from 0.15 to 0.85.

The new coagulopathy profile and imaging findings are explained by Kasabach-Merritt syndrome rather than malignant soft tissue tumor; the infant remains stable without constitutional symptoms. Expert analyses do not support malignancy, so confidence is reduced from 0.10 to 0.05.
